Based on my search, **The Mom Test** is a customer interviewing methodology and book by entrepreneur **Rob Fitzpatrick**, designed to help founders and product managers get honest, actionable feedback about their business ideas—even from people who might otherwise lie to be nice (like your mom).

## Core Concept

The name comes from a relatable scenario: if you ask your mom whether your business idea is good, she'll probably say yes to protect your feelings. The Mom Test teaches you to **ask questions so good that even your mom can't lie to you**.

## The Three Core Rules

1. **Talk about their life, not your idea** — Ask how they currently handle problems, rather than pitching your solution
2. **Ask about specifics in the past, not hypotheticals about the future** — Past behavior reveals truth; questions like "Would you use this?" invite polite lies
3. **Listen more, talk less** — The less you reveal about your idea, the less biased their responses will be

## Why It Matters

Most startups fail because they build products nobody wants. Traditional customer conversations often produce **false positives**—people say nice things that feel validating but lead you in the wrong direction. The Mom Test helps you uncover:
- Real pain points people are actively trying to solve
- Current workarounds and hacks they're already using
- Actual spending patterns (not hypothetical willingness to pay)
- Whether a problem is urgent enough to warrant a solution

## Example Question Shifts

| ❌ Bad (invites lies) | ✅ Good (reveals truth) |
|---|---|
| "Do you like my time-tracking app idea?" | "How do you currently track time on projects? Walk me through it." |
| "Would you pay for scheduling software?" | "Tell me about the last time you struggled with scheduling. What did you do?" |
| "Don't you think this feature is cool?" | "What parts of your current process frustrate you most?" |

The book *The Mom Test: How to Talk to Customers & Learn if Your Business is a Good Idea When Everyone is Lying to You* has become essential reading in startup circles, particularly among indie hackers and Y Combinator-type founders.
